summary:
LAST LIGHT is an interactive web application that explores whether a lunar lander can operate for seven days near the Moon’s south pole. It is designed for students, educators, space enthusiasts, and teams studying the risks of lunar missions.

Users choose a site and start date, then set solar panel power, energy demand, battery capacity, and the maximum allowed interruption of direct Earth contact. The model simulates 168 hours, showing sunlight, Earth visibility, and battery charge. If a plan fails, it identifies the time and cause.

A timeline, horizon chart, and mission start calendar help users compare scenarios and find alternative start dates. Plans can be shared by link, while signed-in users can save their simulation history.

The backend integrates NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides and LRO/LOLA elevation data. A separate 168-hour run using real data is documented in the repository. The interface also supports clearly labeled synthetic demonstration datasets.

Our goal is to make the relationship between terrain, light, energy, and communication easier to understand through experimentation. LAST LIGHT is an educational prototype for preliminary exploration; its simplified models are not certified for flight operations.
details:
What does the project do?
LAST LIGHT simulates the operation of a lunar lander over seven days. Users select an available site, choose a mission start date, and configure the lander’s energy system. The application displays sunlight availability, geometric Earth visibility, battery charge, and the first time the mission violates its specified operating conditions.
The interface combines a timeline, horizon chart, mission start calendar, and explanations of the results. Users can modify their plans, compare alternatives, save simulations, and share scenario parameters through a link.

How does it work?
For each simulated hour, the system compares the elevation of the Sun and Earth with the local terrain horizon in the corresponding direction. This determines whether terrain blocks either body.
The energy model accounts for solar panel output, the lander’s power consumption, and heater demand when that feature is enabled. Battery energy carries forward between hours. The model records a failure when battery charge falls below the selected threshold or when the interruption of direct Earth visibility exceeds the allowed duration.
Interactive calculations run in the browser through a Web Worker. The Django backend provides datasets, authentication, and simulation history. A separate backend API also supports simulations using real ephemerides and elevation maps, including simplified thermal processes and dust effects.

Who is it for, and what benefits does it offer?
LAST LIGHT is intended for students, educators, space hackathon participants, and teams exploring early lunar mission concepts.
Its educational value comes from making cause-and-effect relationships visible. For example, a larger battery may help a lander survive a period of shadow, while a loss of Earth visibility requires a different response. Changing the mission start date may alter both lighting conditions and the final outcome.
Users can test these relationships directly and compare the results of their decisions.
What tools, languages, hardware, and software were used?
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Redux Toolkit, and RTK Query. Charts and the visual scene use SVG, while styling uses CSS Modules.
The backend uses Python, Django, and Django REST Framework. Authentication uses JWT, and data storage uses SQLite. Geospatial processing uses NumPy, Rasterio, and pyproj, while Requests handles external API communication.
Testing uses Vitest, Testing Library, Django’s testing framework, and GitHub Actions. The prototype runs on a standard computer with a web browser and does not require specialized physical hardware.

How was the project created?
We separated the project into a simulation engine, an interactive interface, and backend services. Calculations were implemented as independent functions and background tasks. Shared data structures define sites, mission plans, simulation results, and source information.
Tests cover energy calculations, visibility geometry, error handling, interface behavior, authentication, and simulation history. A separate integration run was completed using real JPL Horizons responses and LOLA elevation data.

What makes the project creative?
LAST LIGHT presents mission planning as an interactive investigation: change a parameter, observe the consequences, understand the cause, and compare another option.
Numerical results are connected to a visual scene, charts, and explanations. Users can explore why a scenario fails and investigate changes that may allow it to meet the selected conditions.

What factors and limitations were considered?
We considered terrain shadowing, available battery energy, power consumption, interruptions of direct Earth visibility, and the availability of input data.
Synthetic demonstration datasets are distinguished from external data. Additional features are shown when the necessary supporting data are available.

Geometric Earth visibility does not replace a radio link budget. The physical models are simplified. Successful integration with NASA data demonstrates that the data-processing workflow runs, but does not independently establish predictive accuracy for a real spacecraft.
